title: “DO NOT AWAKEN LOVE UNTIL IT PLEASES”: Is the Bible Warning Us About Sexual Timing?
paragraphs: “DO NOT AWAKEN LOVE UNTIL IT PLEASES”: Is the Bible Warning Us About Sexual Timing?
We were taught to fear sexual desire. Scripture does something far more beautiful: it teaches us why something this powerful must not be awakened carelessly.
There are some fires you do not extinguish because the fire is evil.
You guard them because the fire is powerful.
And there are some doors you do not refuse to open because what waits behind them is shameful.
You wait because some doors lead into rooms your heart was never meant to enter casually.
That may be one of the most forgotten truths in modern Christianity.
We live in a culture that has learned how to awaken desire before it has learned how to carry covenant.
We know how to flirt before we know how to remain faithful.
We know how to create chemistry before we know how to build character.
We know how to expose bodies before we know how to expose souls.
And sometimes Christians respond by going to the opposite extreme.
We speak about sexual desire as though the desire itself were filthy.
As though attraction were automatically lust.
As though holiness meant becoming emotionally numb.
As though God created the human body, looked at sexuality, became embarrassed by His own design, and then spent the rest of Scripture trying to keep people away from it.
But then you open the Bible...
and you find the Song of Songs.
And suddenly Scripture is speaking about longing.
Beauty.
Desire.
Bodies.
Kisses.
Fragrance.
Touch.
Marriage.
Delight.
Not with pornography’s exploitation.
Not with hookup culture’s disposability.
Not with lust’s selfish hunger.
But with poetry.
Tenderness.
Exclusivity.
Longing.
And astonishing dignity.
Then, right in the middle of all that desire, Scripture repeatedly whispers a warning that sounds almost as though it were written directly to our generation:
“Do not awaken or arouse love until it pleases.”
The Hebrew of Song of Songs 2:7 reads:
הִשְׁבַּ֨עְתִּי אֶתְכֶ֜ם בְּנ֤וֹת יְרוּשָׁלַ֙͏ִם֙ בִּצְבָא֔וֹת א֖וֹ בְּאַיְל֣וֹת הַשָּׂדֶ֑ה אִם־תָּעִ֧ירוּ וְֽאִם־תְּע֥וֹרְר֛וּ אֶת־הָאַהֲבָ֖ה עַ֥ד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּֽץ
Hishba‘ti etkhem benot Yerushalayim... im-ta‘iru ve’im-te‘oreru et-ha’ahavah ‘ad sheteḥpatz.
In a fairly literal sense:
“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem... do not awaken, and do not arouse, love until it desires.”
That refrain does not appear only once.
It returns in Song of Songs 3:5.
And again, with slightly different wording, in 8:4.
Almost as though the Song keeps returning to the same warning:
Love is beautiful.
Desire is powerful.
So do not play with its awakening.
The Hebrew makes the warning especially striking.

The verbs תָּעִירוּ (ta‘iru) and תְּעוֹרְרוּ (te‘oreru) come from the root עוּר (‘ur), associated with waking, stirring, or rousing. The NET translators note that the repeated root gives rhetorical force to the command and that interpreters have understood the image in several related ways—including prematurely forcing romantic love, interfering with passionate love, or stirring sexual passion. In this context, אַהֲבָה (’ahavah, “love”) can carry the force of passionate or sexual desire.
That matters.
Because the Bible is not saying:
“Never awaken love.”
It says:
Do not awaken it until.
There is an until.
And that one word changes everything.
God is not necessarily standing against the fire.
He is teaching His children when the fire belongs in the fireplace.

Sexual desire is not presented throughout Scripture as inherently dirty. Within God’s design, marital intimacy is treated as something honorable; Hebrews 13:4 calls marriage honorable and its bed undefiled. Proverbs 5 even speaks unapologetically about a husband delighting in his wife.
The Song itself eventually gives us one of Scripture’s fiercest descriptions of love:
“For love is strong as death... Many waters cannot quench love.”
That is precisely why love should not be treated like a toy.
You do not hand something “strong as death” to your impulses and say, “Let’s see what happens.”
And perhaps somebody reading this already knows what happens.
You said it was only texting.
Then the conversations moved later into the night.
You said you were only friends.
Then emotional intimacy started creating expectations neither of you had promised to fulfill.
You said it was only flirting.
Only touching.
Only pictures.
Only one night.
Only this once.
And then one morning you discovered that “only” had somehow become attachment.
Now you are trying to forget someone your body remembers.
Trying to stop checking a profile you promised yourself you would stop checking.
Trying not to replay conversations.
Trying to understand why losing someone you were “never technically with” feels strangely like divorce.
Trying to worship while memories you wish you could erase walk through your mind.
Trying to convince yourself that because nobody saw what happened, nothing happened.
But your soul knows.
Your body knows.
Your memories know.
And God knows.
This is where Christians must be careful.

Song of Songs 2:7 is poetry, not a technical manual establishing a precise dating timeline. Faithful interpreters differ over some details of the refrain. We should therefore resist building an entire doctrine of premarital sexuality from this verse alone.
But when the refrain is read alongside the rest of Scripture, a larger biblical sexual ethic becomes unmistakable.
Jesus does not merely address adultery as an outward act; He takes His hearers into the heart and confronts lustful looking in Matthew 5:27–28.
Paul tells believers in 1 Corinthians 6:18 to flee sexual immorality, grounding sexual holiness in the astonishing reality that our bodies belong to Christ.
In 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5, sanctification includes learning to govern sexual desire in holiness and honor rather than being governed by passion.
And Jesus points back to creation when speaking about marriage: male and female, joined together, becoming one flesh.
The Christian vision is therefore much larger than:
“How far can I go before God gets angry?”
That question has already misunderstood holiness.
The better question is:
“How can I love another human being without awakening something I am unwilling or unable to honor?”
Read that again.
Because some of us were not trying to love somebody.
We were trying to use somebody to medicate loneliness.
And we called it love.
We wanted attention.
We wanted reassurance.
We wanted somebody to make us feel attractive again.
We wanted the notifications.
The late-night messages.
The secret conversations.
The feeling of being wanted.
We wanted another human being to silence wounds that should have been brought to Jesus.
And when two wounded people begin asking each other to become saviors, desire can become extraordinarily confusing.
You can feel intensely connected to someone who is profoundly unhealthy for you.
Intensity is not covenant.
Chemistry is not character.
Attention is not faithfulness.
Being desired is not the same thing as being loved.
And sexual access is certainly not proof that someone intends to cherish you.
That distinction is almost revolutionary in a culture where bodies can be exchanged before last names are remembered.
The Gospel says your body has meaning.
Your sexuality has meaning.
The person you desire has meaning.
And because people bear the image of God, nobody should be reduced to a temporary source of pleasure.
This also means Christian sexual boundaries are not supposed to be arbitrary fences erected by frightened religious people.
At their best, boundaries say:
“I refuse to awaken in you what I am not prepared to honor.”
“I refuse to use your loneliness to satisfy mine.”
“I refuse to demand husband privileges while avoiding husband responsibility.”
“I refuse to demand wife privileges while avoiding wife responsibility.”
“I refuse to let tonight create wounds tomorrow will have to carry.”
That is not repression.
That can be love.
Real love does not ask only:
“What do I want from you right now?”
Real love asks:
“What will help you stand before Jesus with greater freedom, greater holiness, and greater joy?”
And suddenly restraint begins looking less like rejection and more like protection.
But perhaps this article has become painful for another reason.
Maybe you did awaken it.
Maybe the warning arrived years too late.
Maybe your story contains sexual sin.
Maybe you gave yourself to somebody who disappeared.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe pornography rewired years of your desires.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once swore you never would.
Maybe there was an affair.
Maybe there was a secret relationship.
Maybe your sexual history feels less like Song of Songs and more like a crime scene.
And every time Christians talk about purity, you feel yourself shrinking.
Because somewhere along the way you started believing the cruelest counterfeit gospel imaginable:
God forgives clean people who made small mistakes.
But not people like me.
Listen carefully.
That is not the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come for people with spotless histories.
He came for sinners.
The cross was not constructed for respectable mistakes.
It was constructed because sin is devastating enough that the Son of God gave Himself to redeem sinners.
Paul reminded the Corinthians of people whose pasts included sexual immorality, adultery, greed, drunkenness and other sins, and then wrote some of the most breathtaking words in the New Testament:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because they rewrote their own history.
Because Christ gave them a new identity.
Paul continues: they had been washed, sanctified and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not renaming sin so repentance becomes unnecessary.
Not celebrating what Christ died to save us from.
But neither is Christianity sentencing forgiven people to lifelong spiritual humiliation.
Repentance says:
“What I did was sin.”
Grace says:
“Sin does not get the final word.”
Repentance brings the darkness into the light.
Grace meets us there.
Repentance stops defending the chains.
Grace breaks them.
And Jesus begins rewriting what shame insisted was already finished.
Maybe your virginity cannot be physically restored.
Maybe certain memories cannot simply be deleted.
Maybe consequences remain.
Maybe somebody broke your heart.
Maybe you broke theirs.
But hear this:
Jesus does not need an untouched past to create a holy future.
The Gospel does not give you a time machine.
It gives you resurrection.
And resurrection is greater.
This is where our theme becomes more than a slogan.
He does not call evil good.
He does something infinitely better.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He teaches.
He transforms.
And He takes people who thought their worst chapter had become the title of their entire life and begins writing something new.
So perhaps the question is not merely:
“Is the Bible warning us about sexual timing?”

Yes, there is genuine wisdom here about refusing to prematurely awaken powerful romantic and sexual desire, and the wider witness of Scripture clearly calls Christians to sexual holiness. But the deeper question is:
Who is controlling what has already been awakened in you?
Your hormones?
Your loneliness?
Pornography?
Your boyfriend?
Your girlfriend?
Your trauma?
Your need to be wanted?
Your fear of losing someone?
Or Jesus?
Because Christianity is not merely about delaying sex.
A person can remain technically abstinent while feeding lust every night.
You can avoid intercourse and still manipulate somebody emotionally.
You can maintain a public image of purity while privately consuming people through a screen.
Biblical holiness reaches deeper.
Jesus wants the heart.
He wants the imagination.
He wants the body.
He wants the secret messages.
He wants the search history.
He wants the wounds beneath the appetite.
He wants the loneliness beneath the compromise.
He wants the shame underneath the hiding.
Not because He is eager to destroy you.
Because He came to make you free.
Maybe tonight your prayer does not need impressive language.
Maybe it needs honesty.
“Jesus, I awakened something I could not control.”
“Jesus, I crossed lines.”
“Jesus, I have been using desire to numb loneliness.”
“Jesus, I still miss someone I know I should release.”
“Jesus, my mind has become polluted.”
“Jesus, I keep returning to pornography.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
That prayer may be more beautiful in heaven than a thousand religious performances.
Because grace begins where pretending ends.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail of your story. But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Sometimes somebody else needs to see that they are not the only Christian still fighting.
And if one particular person came into your mind while reading this, do not ignore that.
Send this privately if their story should remain private.
Save it too.
Because temptation has an interesting way of making us forget in the night what we believed clearly in the morning.
Come back when loneliness starts negotiating.
Come back when an old relationship calls.
Come back when temptation tells you, “Just once.”
Come back and remember:
You are not protecting yourself because desire is worthless.
You guard it because God created sexuality with extraordinary meaning.
But I want to say this carefully because words matter.

Scripture teaches willing, purposeful generosity—not pressured giving. Paul writes that each person should give as he has decided in his heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
Let it be an offering of support, not a transaction with God.
And if you already faithfully set aside giving according to your biblical convictions, do not let us manipulate your conscience into redirecting what you believe belongs elsewhere.
Pray.
Save.
Sometimes supporting the spread of the Gospel costs money.
Sometimes it costs thirty seconds and the courage to let your friends see what you believe.
Neither action purchases God’s approval.
Christ already paid the price we never could.
We serve because we have been loved.
We give because we have received.
We share because somebody else is still hiding in the darkness we once knew.
And perhaps that is the final lesson buried inside those ancient Hebrew words:
אִם־תָּעִירוּ וְאִם־תְּעוֹרְרוּ אֶת־הָאַהֲבָה עַד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּץ
Do not carelessly awaken what was designed to carry enormous power.
Do not treat holy things casually.
Do not confuse desire with destiny.
Do not confuse chemistry with covenant.
Do not let loneliness choose what wisdom would refuse.
But if you already awakened it...
if you already crossed the boundary...
if you already carry the memories...
if the scandal already happened...
then look at the cross.
Because the warning is not the end of the Bible.
Jesus is.
And your sexual past does not possess authority greater than His blood.
Your shame does not outrank His grace.
Your worst night does not get to veto His redemption.
Your scars may explain part of your story.
They do not have to write its ending.
The fire you awakened too soon may have burned pages of your story—but it cannot burn the pen out of the hand of Jesus.
